title: The Four Moves
titleHtml: Turn the insight into a move.
tagline: Translating AI insights into workforce moves.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: learn the four workforce moves, match one AI-exposure insight from your team to the move it calls for, and commit to it with an owner and a date.
heroLead: You mapped the work AI touches most on your team. This session teaches the four workforce moves and commits one of them to an owner and a date.
objectives: Name the four workforce moves: reskill, redeploy, redesign, and hire
Match one AI-exposure insight from your team to the move it calls for
Commit to one move with a named owner and a real date
missionTie: Managers who turn AI signals into real staffing moves are how Exceptional Core Operations keeps its footing while the work itself changes.

agenda.d: Reskill, redeploy, redesign, hire: the whole vocabulary for acting on an AI insight.
Read a real team insight and call the move it asks for.
Make the move real with an owner and a date on the calendar.

manifesto: Match each AI insight to one of the four moves, then give it an owner and a date.

sections.headline: Know your four workforce moves.
sections.lead: When AI changes work on your team, you have four moves. Reskill teaches the new version of the work. Redeploy points a strength where it is needed. Redesign rebuilds the role. Hire buys what you cannot build.
sections.group: In pairs: which of the four moves has your team used most in the last year, and which never? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Which of the four moves has your team used most in the last year, and which never? Write both down.

deeper.title: When the order breaks
deeper.body: The order is a default, not a law. Reskill assumes the person wants the bigger work; some honestly do not, and that answer points you to redeploy. When the receiving work lives on another team, the Transfer Portal is the same move told honestly. A redesign that quietly doubles a role's scope is a hire in disguise. The order has evidence too: McKinsey's skill-gap surveys found reskilling usually beats hiring on cost and fit.
steps: Pick one role where AI changed the routine work. Write all four moves as one line each, even the two that feel wrong for this case.
Cross out the moves the person or the budget truly cannot carry, then write one sentence on why the surviving move wins.

card.text: Try the moves in order of what you already have. Reskill and redeploy work with the people on your team today. Redesign reshapes the role itself. Hire is the move you make when the first three genuinely cannot cover the gap.

interaction.context: In the room: hold one real role from your team in mind, one where AI changed the routine work this year. Walk it through the order: reskill and redeploy use the people you have, redesign reshapes the role, hire covers what the first three cannot. Notice which move your instinct grabbed first.
interaction.discuss: Where has your team jumped straight to hire when reskill or redeploy could have covered it? What made the earlier moves hard to see?
interaction.q: Quick check: your exposure map shows AI now drafts most of a coordinator's routine summaries. What is the first move to consider?

opts.t: Hire a new analyst to handle the higher-level work
opts.why: Hire is the last move in the order, and the most expensive. Start with the person you have; the coordinator freed from summaries is your candidate.

opts.t: Reskill the coordinator toward the review and judgment work AI cannot do
opts.why: Right. The routine work shrank; the judgment work grew. Reskilling the person you already trust is the fastest, cheapest move on the board.

opts.t: Wait for the next annual planning cycle to decide
opts.why: Waiting is the fifth move nobody names, and it is how insights expire. The signal is current now; the move should be too.

sections.headline: One insight, one move.
sections.lead: Read what the signal says about the work, then call the move it asks for. Hire is the reflex and the slowest door: CUPA-HR finds filling positions is supervisors' top challenge.

source.label: Higher ed supervisors on filling positions (CUPA-HR)

sections.group: Breakout pairs: name one insight from your own team, role only, and call its move. Partner challenges it. 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one insight from your own team, role only, and call the move you would make. Then argue for a different move.

deeper.title: Reading a mixed signal
deeper.body: Real signals are rarely pure. Often the routine work shrank and the remaining work changed shape, so reskill and redesign both fit. Sequence them: redesign names the role's new shape first, then reskill grows the person into it. And if you cannot yet say what the role should look like in a year, the match is premature; watch the work for one more month with a date on the recheck. That is patience, not delay.
steps: Take the messiest insight from your exposure map and split it into two sentences: what shrank, and what grew or changed shape.
Call a move for each sentence, then decide which one starts first and write the reason in one line.

interaction.intro: Three team insights, straight from an exposure map like the one you built this spring. Call the move each one asks for; hire stays off the board.
interaction.passMsg: Good reading. The match between signal and move is exactly what your own exposure map needs next.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: reskill when the person should grow with the work, redeploy when a strength needs new work, redesign when the role itself changed shape.

items.q: AI now handles first-pass data cleaning. Your analyst is strong and curious, and the team's real gap is interpretation.
items.why: The person is right; the work moved up a level. Reskilling toward interpretation turns AI's takeover of the routine into a promotion of the human work.

items.q: A scheduler's workload is half gone to automation. The front desk is drowning, and the scheduler is your calmest person with people.
items.why: A freed-up strength plus a starving need on the same team is the classic redeploy. No new skills required; the strength just needs new work to point at.

items.q: AI drafts routine correspondence in a program role. What remains is approvals, exceptions, and relationships: a different job in the old title.
items.why: When the remaining work no longer matches the role's design, rebuild the role. Rewrite it around the human parts, then staff the new shape honestly.

sections.headline: A move needs an owner and a date.
sections.lead: A matched move becomes a workforce action when somebody owns the next step and the step has a date. Build that sentence now, specific enough that anyone could check later whether it happened.

deeper.title: The second sentence
deeper.body: Your move sentence needs a companion most managers skip: the sentence you say to the person whose work is changing. Announced early, a move reads as investment; discovered late, the same move reads as verdict. Draft it in the week you date the move: what you saw change in the work, what you want to grow in them, and what stays theirs. The Oracle 1:1 template holds it well, and that conversation is usually step one anyway.
steps: Draft the three-part opener: what you saw change, what you want to grow, what stays theirs. Keep it to three sentences.
Book the 1:1 where you will say it, inside the same week as your move's dated step one.

interaction.intro: Take one insight-to-move match from your team and make it real. Choose how you state the move and how you anchor it.

opts.t: We should probably look into upskilling opportunities at some point.
opts.coach: No move, no person, no work named. This sentence survives every meeting it attends and changes nothing.

opts.t: The team needs to reskill around AI, starting this quarter.
opts.coach: The move is named and dated, and the who and toward-what are still fog. A move without a specific role and skill is a theme, and themes drift.

opts.t: Reskill our senior coordinator toward exception handling as AI takes the routine casework.
opts.coach: One move, one role, one skill, one reason. Anyone reading this sentence knows exactly what changes and can tell later whether it did.

opts.t: Mention it at a future team meeting when things calm down.
opts.coach: Things never calm down. An anchor with no owner and no date is a wish, and wishes lose to whatever is urgent that week.

opts.t: Add it to your own to-do list to figure out next month.
opts.coach: Better: it exists somewhere. But you own everything on that list already, and next month has no day attached. Give the move its own owner and a Friday.

opts.t: You own step one; the first reskill conversation is on the calendar for Friday.
opts.coach: An owner and a date turn a plan into an appointment. The navigator-led action-planning lab this month is a good place to pressure test it.

heads.strong: A move in motion. The sentence is specific, the owner is named, and Friday makes it real.
heads.mid: A good intention with soft edges. The direction is right; the move still depends on memory.
heads.weak: The insight went back to sleep. Nothing was named, so nothing will be different by fall.

reactions.strong: Two weeks on, the coordinator has started the exception-handling work and says the change finally feels ahead of them instead of chasing them. Your move is now a story other managers borrow.
reactions.mid: A month later the idea resurfaces in a hallway conversation, still healthy, still homeless. It will take one owner and one date to wake it, which is where you started.
reactions.weak: The exposure map is now just a memory. When the role finally changes, it changes to your team instead of with it, and every option left on the table costs more.

recap.q: AI has changed the work in a role on your team. What are your four moves?
recap.why: Reskill the person, redeploy the strength, redesign the role, hire what you cannot build. In roughly that order of cost.

recap.q: A strong performer's routine work is half automated, and another part of the team is understaffed. Best first move?
opts: Wait for the next budget cycle
recap.why: A freed strength next to a starving need is the classic redeploy: fast, cheap, and it tells your best person their value survives the automation.

recap.q: What turns a matched move into a workforce action?
opts: Adding it to the team slide deck
recap.why: Name the move, give step one an owner, and put a date on the calendar. Everything else is documentation.

recapMsgs.high: The vocabulary is loaded. Aim it at one real insight from your team.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Reread the move you were fuzzy on, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Take one more pass through the four moves before you commit to one.

capstone.headline: Match the insight, then date the move.
capstone.lead: Take the sharpest AI insight from your team, role only, never a name. Match it to its move and give it an owner and a date. If none of the three fits, the move is hire; take that one to your HR consultant. Nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: The insight: role and what AI changed about the work.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. program coordinator; AI now drafts most routine correspondence
capstone.practiceLabel: Which move does the insight call for?

practices.name: The reskill move
practices.move: Grow the person toward the work that got bigger: judgment, exceptions, relationships. Book the first conversation.

practices.name: The redeploy move
practices.move: Point the freed-up strength at work that needs it. Name the receiving work and make the introduction.

practices.name: The redesign move
practices.move: Rewrite the role around what stays human, then staff the new shape. Draft the one-paragraph new role description.

whens.out: The move starts this week: owner named and step one on the calendar by Friday.
The move opens your next staff meeting, named out loud with its owner and date.
You bring the move to this month's navigator-led action-planning lab and leave with it pressure tested.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did the move change that the insight alone never would have?

closing.headline: Start the move before Friday.
closing.lead: You leave with the four moves and one of them committed to an owner and a date. This week's Tuesday and Thursday sessions give your team the same discipline for their own work.

closing.nextTitle: Put step one of your move on the calendar
closing.nextBody: Book the first conversation your move requires before Friday. For a longer runway, the LinkedIn Learning course Leading Your Team Through Change by Gemma Leigh Roberts pairs well with this month.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. Assumes the April AI-exposure sessions; June closes the series year with From Insight to Action.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did step one of your move happen? Which move did you call, and would you still call it? What does the owner need from you next?' Count of moves with a named owner and date is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: The four moves
s1.purpose: Install the shared vocabulary: reskill, redeploy, redesign, hire, and the order to try them in.
s1.say: In April you built an exposure map: which work on your team AI touches most. Maps are not moves. This month gives the map a verb, and there are only four worth learning: reskill the person, redeploy the strength, redesign the role, hire what you cannot build. The order matters as much as the list. When McKinsey surveyed companies closing skill gaps, reskilling the people they already had usually beat hiring on both cost and fit, which is why hire sits last today.
facilitate: Walk the four moves once, one line each; resist the urge to lecture.
Read the In the room card aloud; everyone holds one real role in mind and names their instinct move silently.
Lead the discussion prompt, two or three voices, then run the breakout: which move most, which never?

ask.q: Which of the four moves does your team reach for first, honestly?
expect: Hire, because it feels like the real solution
Reskill, because training requests are easy to make
ask.respond: Most rooms admit to hire-first. The order flips that default: the cheapest moves use the people already on your team.

s1.debrief: Four verbs, tried in order of what you already have. That order is the discipline of this month.
s1.watchFor: Managers treating the moves as HR paperwork categories. Keep them as verbs a manager can start this week.
s1.transition: Vocabulary done. Now the skill: matching a real insight to its move.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; take two discussion answers in chat.

s2.title: The match
s2.purpose: Practice matching an AI-exposure insight to the move it calls for.
s2.say: Here is the skill this month actually asks of you: read what a signal says about the work, then call the move. We will do three together. Notice that hire is off the board for all three; that is deliberate. Hire is real, and it comes after the other three have been honestly tried.
facilitate: Run Call the move live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause: ask who called it differently and why. The disagreement is the teaching.
Run the breakout: one real insight, role only, partner challenges the call.

ask.q: Why is redeploy the least used move in most departments?
expect: We think in roles, so freed capacity looks like slack
Managers fear losing the person to another team
ask.respond: Both true. Redeploy asks you to see strengths as portable. The Transfer Portal thinking from the fall applies inside your own team too.

s2.debrief: Reskill grows the person with the work. Redeploy points a strength at new work. Redesign rebuilds the role. Say the reason out loud when you call the move; the reason is the match.
s2.watchFor: Anyone naming a struggling teammate by name in the breakout. Redirect warmly: roles, never names.
s2.transition: You can call the move. Now it needs an owner and a date, or it stays a slide.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, one voice on the debrief.

s3.title: Owner and date
s3.purpose: Convert one matched move into a sentence with an owner and a date.
s3.say: The distance between an insight and an action is one sentence: the move, a role, a reason, then an owner and a date. Vague versions of that sentence survive meetings for years. We are going to build the sharp version and put step one on a real calendar.
facilitate: Run Write the move; give the room two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read a strong outcome aloud.
Point at the pattern: specific sentence, named owner, dated step one.

ask.q: Why does 'the team needs to reskill around AI' fail as a move?
expect: No person, no skill, no date
Nobody can tell later whether it happened
ask.respond: Right. A move you cannot verify later was never a move. Specific enough to check is the bar.

s3.debrief: One sentence, one owner, one date. If it will not fit that shape, it is still an insight.
s3.watchFor: Owners who are always the manager. Push at least step two toward the person whose work is changing; it is their move too.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own move card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now the real one. Take the sharpest insight from your April exposure map, role only. Call its move, name the owner, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: This series year opened with seeing talent. It wraps this month with moving on what you see. Hold step one this week. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday has everyone, your team included, building a personal 90-day AI action plan; point your people at it. Thursday's Thrive Thursday wraps the series year with decisiveness, moving from data to move, which is this exact muscle. And for a longer runway, this month's LinkedIn Learning course, Leading Your Team Through Change, and the navigator-led action-planning lab are built for the move you just wrote.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager says every insight on their map points to hire
contingencies.then: Run the order out loud: what would reskill look like here, what would redeploy look like, what would redesign look like? Hire earns its place only after those three answers exist.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real person while matching an insight to a move
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' The moves work on work, and the traffic light is firm: private information about people is red, never.

toughQuestions.q: Doesn't redesign just mean cutting jobs?
toughQuestions.a: Redesign here means rebuilding a role around the work that stays human: judgment, exceptions, relationships. Done early and openly, it protects people from the quiet version, where the role hollows out and the person gets blamed for it. Position changes are a separate process with HR; this session is how you avoid needing one.

toughQuestions.q: Can I use AI tools to analyze my team's data and pick the move?
toughQuestions.a: Run it through the traffic light. Generic scenarios and public research: green, go. Internal workload data: yellow, approved VU tools only. Anything private about individual people, their performance, health, or circumstances: red, never. The move decision itself stays human; it is a judgment call about people you know.

toughQuestions.q: What if my move needs budget or a requisition I don't control?
toughQuestions.a: Then step one is the ask, owned and dated like any other step. A specific sentence with a role, a reason, and a date is exactly what gets funded; vague reskilling themes are what get deferred. Bring it to the action-planning lab and your HR consultant with the sentence already written.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on turning your AI map into a move. Dust off the AI-exposure map you built this spring, or just bring one honest observation about how AI has changed work on your team this year. Roles only, never names. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the move start? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did step one of the move on your card happen? 2) Which move did you call, and would you still call it? 3) What does the owner of the next step need from you?
